title: SULEJMANOVIC et SULTANOVIC contre l'ITALIE
conclusion: Partiellement recevable;Partiellement irrecevable (Art. 35) Conditions de recevabilité;(Art. 35-3-a) Ratione materiae
summary:
In the case of Sulejmanovic and Sultanovic v. Italy, the applicants were four members of an extended family of Roma origin from Bosnia-Herzegovina, including Paso and Hadzira Sulejmanovic, their son Nenad, and his wife Halida Sultanovic. The family, who identified as “Tziganes” (a term historically used for Roma), fled the war in the former Yugoslavia and settled in Italy, making their home in the Casilino 700 camp in Rome.

The case centred on the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller families facing expulsion and precarious living conditions. The applicants alleged that their forced removal from Italy exposed them, as Roma, to a real risk of inhuman or degrading treatment upon return to Bosnia-Herzegovina, where Roma communities faced discrimination, poverty, and social exclusion.

After arriving in Italy in the early 1990s, the family lived in the Casilino 700 camp, which was overcrowded and lacked basic sanitation. In 1999 and 2000, Italian authorities conducted police checks and issued expulsion orders against the applicants, citing irregular immigration status and lack of legal income. The applicants challenged these measures, arguing that their expulsion would violate Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life), and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The European Court of Human Rights declared the case partially admissible, finding that the applicants’ complaints under Article 3 warranted further examination due to the complex factual and legal issues involved. However, other aspects were found inadmissible for failure to exhaust domestic remedies or as being outside the Court’s jurisdiction.

This case is significant as it highlights the precarious situation of Roma and Traveller families in Europe, particularly those displaced by conflict and facing exclusion both in their countries of origin and in host states. It reflects the broader historical context of systemic discrimination and marginalisation experienced by Roma and Travellers across the continent.
